source.title: A Universal Class of Sharpness-Aware Minimization Algorithms
source.authors: B. Tahmasebi; Ashkan Soleymani; Dara Bahri; S. Jegelka; Patrick Jaillet

record.file_problem: Text contains the full paper, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains sharpness-aware objectives and measures resulting test accuracy and Hessian sharpness. This conceptually tests whether the measured sharpness property tracks generalization, but it does not measure the train–test error gap as defined in V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Frob-SAM Hessian-norm trajectories and test accuracy, plus benchmark test-accuracy comparisons among sharpness-aware methods. These results bear on V7's measured-sharpness/generalization relationship, but do not compare train–test gaps for similarly low-training-loss networks. Other sharpness minimizers and optimizer comparisons are not rows for V7 unless they measure its named relationship. The table's flattened layout makes some method-to-value assignments uncertain.
record.test_reason: The study develops sharpness-aware training objectives and evaluates their optimization bias and test accuracy. It does not test V7's relationship between magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and train–test gaps among comparably fitted networks. Its other experiments do not test V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors establish a universally expressive Hessian-based sharpness framework, prove corresponding objectives' explicit optimization biases under stated assumptions, and report practical accuracy benefits in some settings, especially limited-data and noisy-label regimes. They leave identifying the best bias for each task open.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces sharpness-aware objectives targeting Hessian measures, rather than measuring magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness against the training–test gap. It reports test accuracy and sharpness trajectories, not the relationship specified by V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset regime (full, 10% subsampled, or 20% corrupted training labels), sharpness algorithm, regularization strength, and perturbation parameter vary across experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 shows that stronger Frob-SAM regularization produces lower Hessian Frobenius norms during MNIST training; every setting exceeds 94% final test accuracy. This establishes an optimization bias, without measuring the specified sharpness–gap relationship.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frob-SAM explicitly reduces the Hessian Frobenius norm during training.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 2–3 compare sharpness-aware methods with SGD using ResNet18 test accuracy. On CIFAR10 with 20% corrupted training labels, Frob-SAM reaches 87.57±0.10%, versus 85.42±0.08% for SAM and 82.78±0.20% for SGD. These are method-performance comparisons without magnitude-aware sharpness or train–test gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Particular sharpness-aware training objectives can improve test accuracy, with benefits depending on the dataset and training regime.

record.problems: The experiment linking sharpness and generalization is a single MNIST network and reports the Hessian Frobenius norm trajectory and final test accuracy, not a train–test gap or a comparison across networks. Benchmark tables report test accuracy and standard errors, but the extracted table layout is flattened.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows: Figure 2 reports Hessian Frobenius norm by regularization strength and says all settings exceed 94% final test accuracy, but this does not measure the train–test gap or the relationship among similarly low-training-loss networks required by V7. Tables 2 and 3 compare test accuracy across algorithms and datasets, not the V7 relationship.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed random-label training, including training fit and held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; ASAM is a sharpness-aware method, not this optimizer comparison.
Large versus small batches under matched epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on training-set size or augmentation.

Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness versus train–test error gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, including ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. The Hessian counterexamples concern unnormalized measures and do not refute this version.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Change the record's tests/T2 classification to uses_without_test/T4 and V7 to not tested. Keeping the result rows empty is appropriate; the nonqualifying experiments are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparisons.

The study measures sharpness during training and reports test accuracy, but does not measure train–test gaps among networks with similarly low training loss or compare magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness with the named alternative measures.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples.
